html:
N'Ko is an alphabet for the Manding languages of West Africa, such as Bambara, Maninka and Dyula. It was created in 1949 by Solomana Kanté, a teacher from Guinea. N'Ko means "I say" in all the Manding languages.

Kanté was working as a trader in Côte d'Ivoire when he read a claim that African languages could not be written properly. He tried writing Maninka in the Arabic and Latin scripts and found that neither marked its tones and sounds well. So he made his own alphabet. Like Arabic it runs right to left and its letters join at the base, but it marks every vowel and tone.

Kanté then spent his life writing in N'Ko: grammars, histories of the Mali Empire, medicine, and a translation of the Quran. The script spread by people teaching each other, not through the state, and it became a symbol of cultural pride.

It is used today in Guinea, Mali and among Manding speakers abroad, in books, newspapers, websites and phones. It stands with the Vai syllabary and the Bamum script among Africa's modern inventions in writing.
